subject: burtonCat
pitch:
Category: Animal.
Subject: skinny black cat with spiral tail.
Style: Tim Burton.
reasoning:
I'm planning a TypeScript module for a Tim Burton-style illustration of a gaunt black cat with a spiral tail—thinking through gaunt limbs, oversized eyes with dark circles, stitched details, and a pale grey-purple palette with spiral motifs for the eyes and tail.

Now I'm sketching the skeleton structure: defining joint positions for hips, spine, neck, and head to create a standing pose with exaggerated proportions—long skinny legs, a tall gaunt body around 0.42 shoulder height, and a coiled spiral tail.

Building the skeleton hierarchy...

Still defining joint chains...

For the ribs, I'm working out which side of the tube corresponds to "left" versus "right" by reasoning about angle direction relative to the tube's running axis, then placing paired rib arcs using curve points sampled at specific angles along each rib position.

Now I'm reconsidering the torso's overall proportions, deciding the spine chain should run longer (hips to chest) so the rib region sits in a more natural stretch of the body before it transitions into the neck and head.

For the legs, I'm working out an IK setup with shoulder, elbow, wrist, and paw joints, giving the front limbs long spindly segments with bent elbows pointing backward for that Burton-esque skeletal look.

I'll go with those lengths since too-long chains just bend more, while too-short would be the actual problem. For feet, I'm placing paw targets near the ground at the paw's radius height, naming the chain joints shoulder→elbow→wrist→paw with a left/right suffix determined by whether the joint's x-coordinate is positive.

I'll mostly use world coordinates for placement to avoid confusion over which side "local x" maps to. For the leg sweep, I'm setting a radius profile that's thicker near the hip and tapers toward the wrist before widening slightly again at the paw.

For paws, I'm going with a small flattened sphere shape plus three tiny forward-pointing toe capsules to keep that pointy Burton-esque silhouette. I'm also considering pale stripe accents on the legs and tail over the base black color, nodding to that classic striped Burton look.

Writing the coat paint function...

For the tail, I'm shaping a flat spiral coil rising from the rump in a vertical plane, Burton-style, using a spiral path with adjustable turns and radius.

Working out the spiral's center and starting radius so the coil connects smoothly to a curved base path leading from the rump up into the spiral itself.

Working out the spiral geometry with a shrinking radius from 0.13 to 0.035 over 1.75 turns, centered near (0, 0.66, -0.5), and checking the base path points stay clear of the rump at z=-0.3 with its 0.07 radius.

I think it's more reliable to manually sample points along the spiral and feed them into a catmull curve instead of relying purely on parametric math -- building a joined list of base points plus spiral points sampled every 30°, then chaining tail joints with a count of 9 named tail1 through tail9.

Working out the spiral geometry...

To avoid a flat spring look, I'm adding a slight x-offset that grows with the angle so the coil becomes gently conical, with pitch sized against the tube radius to prevent self-intersection. For the tail, I'm planning alternating lilac and black stripe bands starting partway along the length, painted based on position.

Checking proportions now: the tail coil ends up taller than the cat's body, so I'm shrinking the coil radius and lowering its center to keep things cartoonishly balanced while still whimsical. Then I'm working out the neck and head placement, sizing the skull larger than realistic for that stylized big-head look.

For the head itself, I'll compute coordinates relative to the head joint rather than fixed world positions, since the head tilts slightly forward. I'm picturing a wide, flat-topped skull with huge wide-set eyes, a tiny pointed muzzle, and tall pointed ears to match that Burton-esque design.

The eyes are the real focal point — big round shapes with a chartreuse iris, dark ring, and a spiral pupil instead of a simple slit, drawn as an SVG decal applied to the skull surface.

I'll make the texture transparent outside the circle so only the eye shows against black fur, and add a sunken lilac-gray ring around each eye for that Burton-style dark circle effect. Now I'm working out the decal placement parameters for positioning the eyes on the model.

Using the surface hit as the decal position, with azimuth set to s*34 and elevation 4 so eyes sit wide-set and symmetric. Since the default normal-based direction would make the eyes look outward too much, I'll override dir to something closer to forward-facing so they project onto the surface undistorted.

Now for the muzzle: a tiny sphere for the Burton-style snout near the lower front of the head, with a small dark triangular nose extruded forward using a simple outline shape, keeping proportions subtle and compact.

For the mouth, I'm separating the jaw into its own hinged part—a small wedge joint near the lower head aimed forward—and considering whether a stitched smile should sit across both jaws or just stay fixed since stitching across the hinge would look broken when the jaw opens.

I'm settling on a thin crooked "ω"-shaped mouth line painted directly onto the muzzle sphere, in pale lilac, with three tiny stitch ticks for that classic sewn-smile look, keeping it contained to the muzzle so it doesn't overlap the skull.

Now moving to the ears — tall, pointed, and tilted outward, built from an extruded triangular outline with a ragged torn notch cut into one edge, mirrored across the x-axis. I'm working out the extrusion axes so the tilt reads correctly in a front view.

s,-0.3,0], y=[0.3*s,1,0], checking the dot products stay orthogonal for both s values.
